newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Nordics facing different currency policy paths.
newsitem.headline: Nordics facing different currency policy paths.

text.p: The Nordic countries, in the past often grouped together by foreign investors, now seem to be making different currency policy choices -- reflecting diverse political and economic realities at home.
Sweden, Denmark, Finland and Norway share close cultural, commercial and linguistic ties but appear to be going their own ways when it comes to currencies.

"They are very different, although they are all put in one lump. They have different choices, different political constraints," said Beshara Madi, international economist at investment bank Morgan Stanley in London.
The three Nordic European Union members -- Denmark, Finland and Sweden -- have shown varying degrees of enthusiasm for monetary union, due to start in 1999.
Finland is determined to be among the first to join economic and monetary union (EMU); Denmark has decided to stay out; Sweden is hesitating.
The Finnish markka and the Swedish crown are currently floating following the European currency turmoil in 1992 and the Danish crown is in the EU's exchange rate mechanism (ERM).
Norway, which rejected membership of the EU in a 1994 referendum, has a managed float for its crown and seeks to maintain a stable exchange rate against European currencies.
Economist Katharina Hoyland at J P Morgan said the Nordics used to be grouped together for geographical reasons.
But, she said, "sophisticated investors have realised over the past decade or so that there is a different story in each one of those countries."
Just as other European countries opted for different currency regimes "the various Nordic countries opt for different stances based on domestic politics and economics," she said.
Economist Carl B. Hamilton at Handelsbanken in Stockholm took a similar line, saying there were separate currency strategies.
"So it would be wise for an investor to have a differentiated view on the Nordics as four different markets in the coming five to six years, not least because of the currency policies," he said.
Finland and Sweden both joined the EU on January 1, 1995, but have since displayed different attitudes towards EMU.
This was evident last week when Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink said Sweden could delay its entry into EMU.
His comments also strengthened the view that Sweden would not join the ERM quickly, even if Finland goes ahead soon.
"If Finland and Italy join (the ERM), then only Sweden, Britain and Greece will stand outside the European currency cooperation," Swedish bank Nordbanken said in a report.
Madi at Morgan Stanley said Finnish EU enthusiasm was largely explained by it being a neighbour of Russia.
"It explains why they are playing it by the rule and they want to be in the first group that starts EMU," he said.
Sweden did not have the same consensus on the issue.

"There is quite a divergence of views among the electorate and in particular in the (ruling) Social Democratic Party and therefore there isn't the same amount of enthusiasm to be part of EMU," Madi said.
Denmark, with one of the strongest economies in Europe, rejected EMU in a 1993 referendum. A new plebiscite would be needed to overturn that decision.
However, these differences in Nordic currency policies may turn out to be only temporary.
"It seems to be the case for both Denmark and Sweden that joining in 1999 is not an issue at the moment because of political considerations but it could be in, for example, 2002," Madi said.
As it is not in the 15-nation EU, Oslo cannot decide to join EMU but Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland has said it should somehow be coupled with the single currency.
However, oil-rich Norway is in a special situation, being heavily influenced by the oil market.
